sources.title: Yakuza Series Creator Toshiro Nagoshi's Studio Has Officially Shut Down Before Releasing a Game
sources.text: Yakuza series creator Toshiro Nagoshi’s studio has officially shut down before it had the chance to release a game. Gematsu reported that the Tokyo-based Nagoshi Studio closed its doors via a shareholders’ resolution on October 31. The announcement was made in today’s Japanese government gazette Kanpo. The Yakuza-like Gang of Dragon was meant to be the debut game from Nagoshi Studio, which Nagoshi formed in 2022 with investment from Chinese megacorp NetEase after he departed Ryu Ga Gotoku a year earlier. But doubt was cast on its future in March when NetEase signalled its intention to cut off funding as part of a broader retreat from international video game investment. According to Bloomberg , NetEase made the decision to cut Nagoshi’s funding after it learned Gang of Dragon needed at least another ¥7 billion (approx. $44.4 million) to be completed. Nagoshi was apparently trying to find new investors to help buy the studio out, without much luck. The studio closes nearly a year after Gang of Dragon enjoyed a flashy reveal at The Game Awards in December . Now, it looks like it may never see the light of day. sources.text: Nagoshi Studio revealed Gang of Dragon less than a year ago, but it ran into trouble just a few months later. Six months after the disappearance of Nagoshi Studio's website, a Google-translated notice in the Japan government's Kanpo website (via Gematsu ) says the company has now officially closed its doors. Founded by Yakuza creator Toshihiro Nagoshi in 2021 after a run of more than 30 years at Sega, Nagoshi Studio's first game was revealed at the 2025 Game Awards as Gang of Dragon—although the reveal was really just a brief CGI clip of Ma Dong-Seok that could have been lifted straight from Korean action film The Outlaws. The wheels came off just a few months later, though, when NetEase pulled funding for the studio, amidst a broader pullback from external studio support over the previous year. Nagoshi Studio reportedly had no success finding another benefactor to fill the gap, and two months later, in May, the studio's website disappeared . No official proclamations about the fate of the studio were forthcoming, though, and the Steam page remained online, so faint hope of a last-minute rescue persisted. sources.title: Gang of Dragon developer Nagoshi Studio shutters months after NetEase cut funding
sources.text: Studio was "officially dissolved by a shareholders' resolution" on October 31, 2026 Gang of Dragon developer Nagoshi Studio has been closed after NetEase withdrew funding earlier this year. According to Gematsu , the Japanese government gazette Kanpo published a closure notice on October 31, stating the studio was "officially dissolved by a shareholders' resolution." Yakuza series creator Toshihiro Nagoshi founded Nagoshi Studio under NetEase Games in 2022 . In December 2025, the studio debuted a teaser trailer for its new IP, Gang of Dragon, at The Game Awards. By March 2026, NetEase confirmed it had cut funding to the studio but did not disclose reasons or exit terms. Reports indicated NetEase estimated "at least ¥7 billion ($44.4 million) more would be needed" for Nagoshi Studio to complete Gang of Dragon. The developer reportedly "tried to find new sponsors without success" and NetEase told it that "while it is free to continue on its own, it must bear the corresponding costs if it wants to keep the assets or brand." Nagoshi joined Sega in 1989 and spent several years in the AM2 arcade division. He later served as chief creative officer at Sega until 2021, after stepping down from the board . Nagoshi continued at Sega as creative director and was also general director of Like a Dragon developer Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio. Nagoshi Studio is not the only Japanese developer to have ended its partnership with NetEase. In September, Romeo is a Dead Man Grasshopper Manufacture split from the China-based publisher to become independent . CEO Goichi 'Suda51' Suda said the studio "found a strong desire to deliver titles in an even wider variety of styles to video game lovers everywhere," which led it to become independent again. "This decision was reached after thorough discussions with NetEase Games and with their generous cooperation. We continue to cherish the amazing relationship our companies have built, and look forward to further collaboration when the opportunity arises."

sources.text: NetEase reportedly pulled funding earlier this year Nagoshi Studio – the developer founded by Yakuza and Super Monkey Ball creator Toshihiro Nagoshi – has been shut down. Following the release of series semi-reboot Yakuza: Like a Dragon and Lost Judgement, Nagoshi departed Sega after an over 30-year career at the company, founding Nagoshi Studio alongside Yakuza series director Daisuke Sato. The NetEase studio remained pretty quiet until The Game Awards in 2025 where its debut title Gang of Dragon was unveiled with a trailer starring Train to Busan and soon-to-be Physint star Ma Dong-seok. Earlier this year, reports emerged that NetEase was pulling funding on the game after reportedly discovering it would need an extra 7 billion yen in funding, following the developer's YouTube channel and website being taken down, as well as Sato changing his Twitter bio to say ex-Nagoshi Studio, leaving the game and studio's future in doubt. Now, just over five years since Nagoshi left Sega, a notice posted in Japanese government gazette Kanpo (via Gematsu ) confirms that Nagoshi Studio was dissolved on October 31. NetEase has been pulling back on investments over the last year or two, with Worlds Untold – founded by Mass Effect writer Mac Walters – and Jar of Sparks – founded by former Halo lead Jerry Hooks – having their funding pulled. Meanwhile, Suda 51-founded Grasshopper Manufacture self-published its most recent title – Romeo Is a Dead Man – despite being owned by NetEase, with the studio splitting from the publisher to go independent just over a month ago. Neither Nagoshi or the studio has been active on social media since the start of the year, so no official word has been made by the developer. sources.title: Nintendo Reveals Development Team Behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake
sources.text: Nintendo has revealed the development team responsible for creating The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . The Super Mario Bros. company typically keeps its cards pretty close to its chest when it comes to the behind-the-scenes details for its biggest releases. The Legend of Zelda series is no exception, but Nintendo did offer a peek behind the curtain as part of an Ocarina of Time remake installment in its Ask the Developer Q&A series. Fans have speculated who might be behind the Nintendo Switch 2 reimagining of an all-time classic since it was announced. While some believed Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft might be leading the charge, for example, the interview confirmed that it's actually Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EDP) Production Group No. 3 that's responsible for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. Featured in the first interview chapter are franchise producer Eiji Aonuma and series directing veteran Hidemaro Fujibayashi, with EDP Production Group No. 3's HokWai Ng, Aya Shida, Hiroki Taguchi, and Masato Ohashi also listed as interviewees to be featured in future highlights. In other words, the core team behind one of the most highly-anticipated games of the last few years is the same group behind most The Legend of Zelda projects from the last 30 years. Longtime fans of the original Nintendo 64 game (or even its 2011 Nintendo 3DS remake) who have feared the Switch 2 version of the story could tarnish its reputation can probably rest easy knowing it was in experienced hands. That said, it is always possible another team like Monolith Soft could have chipped in as a support developer, though we likely won't know the full list of team members until we have a better look at those credits in a few days. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches for Switch 2 November 5. Although it was made by the same hands that have helped keep the classic fantasy franchise kicking for decades, that doesn't mean the developers weren't willing to experiment where they could. During the interview, Aonuma explained that he tried to "basically let the developers make whatever changes they genuinely felt were necessary." "I wanted the team to make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time their own, and to follow through on their own ideas about what the game should be," he added. "That said, I did deliver my fair share of lectures along the way. (Laughs) I took a step back to observe how the younger members of the development team would reimagine The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using the insights and answers they had arrived at on their own." Fujibayashi added that, from his point of view, it was important for the team to have a clear outline for what would and wouldn't be changed from the Nintendo 64 game early on. "For people like us, who know both the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and the recent 3D Legend of Zelda games, there's no shortage of things we’d like to say when it comes to designing a game," he said. "(Laughs) That’s why I took a step back and supported the team from a broader perspective by helping them clarify the things they needed to be mindful of when designing the game." Despite having a good plan for how Nintendo and EDP Production Group No. 3 would tackle The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake from the get-go, Aonuma recently admitted that he's still a bit nervous to see how fans will respond . sources.title: Nintendo Explains Why It Chose to Do Another The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake
sources.text: Nintendo has explained why it chose to develop another The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . Franchise producer Eiji Aonuma was asked what sparked the team's desire to return to one of the most treasured stories in gaming history during the first installment in a series of Ask the Developer Q&A posts. It's an in-depth chat about what it was like to revisit a classic game for Nintendo Switch 2, and how it came about in the first place. The reimagining set to launch in just a few short days will mark the second time Nintendo has remade The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (the first launched for the Nintendo 3DS in 2011 ). Aonuma explained that there were a number of factors Entertainment Planning & Development (EDP) Production Group No. 3 had in mind, with its 40th anniversary being one of the most important. "This year marks the 40th anniversary of the very first Legend of Zelda game," Aonuma said. "With that in mind, I was thinking about what I should create as the producer of the series. Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles. That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'" Aonuma makes a good point. Although he worked on the original Nintendo 64 game when it launched in 1998 and has carried that experience through subsequent entries in the series in the decades since, there are plenty of team members who don't have that same familiarity with its past. Sure, there are those with a passing familiarity with the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time or those who have at least played it, but Aonuma started to wonder how they'd interpret the game "as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games." Allowing them to not only revisit that original story but also leave their own stamp on it, he believes, could help bolster whatever new The Legend of Zelda games come next. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake," he added, "it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development. If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again." Aonuma elaborated, saying that there were many elements considered when choosing to develop a The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2. The team wanted players who had grown used to the open structure of games like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom to enjoy the fun of "progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story" that is "gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way." Nintendo's latest The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches for Switch 2 November 5. Despite having decades of experience and solid reasoning backing the decision to do a remake, Aonuma recently said he's still "nervous" to see what players think . While we wait to get our hands on the launch build, you can see what IGN thought in our hands-on preview . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. sources.text: The Nintendo Switch 2 is the talk of the town this week, not just because stock hunters are ready and waiting for its first special edition release but also while we count down the final days until its biggest release of the year so far. The Nintendo Switch 2 has dropped from $499 to $469 at the Amazon-owned retailer, but this one's going to move fast. I've previously only ever seen discounted refurbished units on these shelves and even they typically sell out before the day is done. While we're still not at the $449 launch price of the handheld, Woot's $30 saving represents one of the first Nintendo Switch 2 deals to drop after the price increased in September. Woot has sold Nintendo Switch 2 handhelds cheaper than this in the past, but rarely in new condition and this is the first time I've seen it here since the September 1 price increase. Refurbished handhelds swallow up this shelf space every now and then, with the most recent offering landing back in October. Combining an on-screen discount with an additional discount tied to its gaming event, customers could grab renewed devices for as little as $409. That was a perfect storm of savings we see typically once or twice a year. If you're upgrading your handheld ahead of Ocarina of Time (while still spending as little as possible), Woot's current Nintendo Switch deal will get you there for $50 less than the hard-to-find special edition release. The discount is our GamesRadar+ Deal of the Day for November 2, but judging by the speed at which renewed offers have flown off the shelves at Woot it's not expected to last much longer. sources.title: Google's new Zelda: Ocarina of Time Easter egg takes us back to 1998 in time for Nintendo's remake
sources.text: Google is gearing up for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake as much as any of us, it seems, with a nostalgic little Easter egg. For years now, Google has included some fun Easter eggs via its search engine. You can type "Minecraft" into your browser to play a bit of the iconic Mojang game. Or, input "do a barrel roll" and watch your screen flip around. The latest Easter egg from Google offers no exception, acting as a silly (but very welcome) ode to Nintendo's beloved Zelda franchise – simply type in "The Legend of Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time" and see for yourself. A Master Sword will appear, and should you click on it, you'll see it inserted – and then you'll be transported back to 1998, when Nintendo's original Ocarina of Time made its way into the wild, sort of like a pseudo-child Link or something. The old Google font, bright primary colors, and exclamation mark intact, is there, along with the 90s search interface you might recall from way back when. The whimsy is unparalleled, honestly. I'm not the only one obsessed with it, either (seriously, you don't want to know how many times I've searched for Zelda today so far). Over on X , comments see folks agreeing that it's a good bit of fun – and, uh, unsurprisingly wishing that Google's search engine still looked like it did in 1998. As one reads, "Can we just… keep it like that now? Forever." Another adds, "Can we get that Google back?" Sadly, though, I think we're stuck as adult Link in 2026. This is all in honor of the Ocarina of Time remake anyway, which is set to release in just a few days on November 5. It boasts everything that made us fall in love with the OG some 28 years ago while also bringing new features to the table, from sidequests to dungeon tweaks and Breath of the Wild's option to turn off the UI for more immersion (and difficulty). Plus, breathe a sigh of relief – the jump button we've wanted for decades. Not all Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake devs have played the N64 original, series producer says – but "it's thanks to these young people" it was made Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week After spending years with her head in various fantastical realms' clouds, Anna studied English Literature and then Medieval History at the University of Edinburgh, going on to specialize in narrative design and video game journalism as a writer. She has written for various publications since her postgraduate studies, including Dexerto, Fanbyte, GameSpot, IGN, PCGamesN, and more. When she's not frantically trying to form words into coherent sentences, she's probably daydreaming about becoming a fairy druid and befriending every animal or she's spending a thousand (more) hours traversing the Underdark in Baldur's Gate 3. If you spot her away from her PC, you'll always find Anna with a fantasy book, a handheld video game console of some sort, and a Tamagotchi or two on hand. sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Studio Officially Revealed
sources.text: It looks like the usual suspects are handling the upcoming remake Nintendo is infamously cagey about revealing which studios are working on its games. While the company’s secrecy isn’t entirely out of step with an industry that generally hides how the sausage is made, Nintendo takes this to another level, trying to create a Disneyland-like sense of wonder around its brand. After speculation that a support studio is handling the upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake , an Ask the Developer article posted by Nintendo officially confirms which team is leading development: longtime Zelda studio Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3. Of the six developers interviewed, four are from Production Group No. 3. The other two are Eiji Aonuma, longtime Zelda producer and the former group manager of Group No. 3, and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who directed several Zelda games at the studio. While it seems fairly obvious that the new Zelda game is being worked on by the studio that makes most of The Legend of Zelda games, there were several reasons to doubt that. For starters, the previous remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the 3DS wasn't made by Production Group No. 3, and was instead handled by the Japanese studio Grezzo. That team also made the 3DS version of Majora’s Mask and led development on 2024’s The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom . Another popular candidate for leading development on the Ocarina of Time remake was Xenoblade creator Monolith Soft. Nintendo owns Monolith Soft, and it acted as a support studio on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom , The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild , and others. Monolith is currently developing Xenoblade Genesis , which is scheduled for a 2027 release on the Nintendo Switch 2. While some will undoubtedly be disappointed that the main Zelda team is working on a remake instead of fully dedicating itself to the next major installment in the series, it's possible it is doing both with the help of support studios. Additionally, if Grezzo and Monolith aren’t working on this remake, they may have more time for other projects, like a potential follow-up to Echoes of Wisdom and the previously mentioned Xenoblade title. We’ll find out the full list of studios that contributed to the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake when the game comes out on Nov. 5.

sources.title: Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"
sources.text: "I thought we needed to address this in this new version." The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty , for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel. In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old. "In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said. "I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again." There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives. Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development." As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style , art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake .

sources.text: A video reel showcasing what appears to be work-in-progress footage of a Revelations: Persona remake has surfaced online. The footage, a showreel similar to the one showcasing footage of Persona 3 Reload that leaked prior to its announcement, features three sections of the game—field, battle, and event scenes built around 2D illustrations. Persona 2: Innocent Sin protagonist Tatsuya Suou appears in the battle section of the footage. However, since he does not appear in Revelations: Persona , he may be a stand-in for another character. It’is also possible that remakes of Persona 2: Innocent Sin and / or Persona 2: Eternal Punishment are simultaneously in development. Other things worth noting are the constant appearance of Unreal Engine debut text in the upper-left corner of the screen and the fact that Eriko Kirishima appears to use the same Persona summon animation as Yukiko Amagi in Persona 4 Revival , lending the footage further credibility. As for the source of the footage, it was originally posted to YouTube by a user named “P1REMAKE” today at 2:25 a.m. PT / 5:25 a.m. ET . As of press time, the YouTube video remains accessible, but copies have also been hosted on file-sharing websites such as Gofile and Catbox , and shared in communities like r/GamingLeaksAndRumours . sources.text: The producer of Persona 4 Revival recently said Persona 1 and 2 remakes should happen A trailer for a remake of the original Persona appears to have leaked online. The footage, which was shared on YouTube without warning by a new account,Â appears to show a montage consisting of gameplay footage, combat and dialogue. It also appears similar to the recent Persona 3 and 4 remakes, but with a modiifed UI, and contains remixed versions of music from the original game. While these days there’s always the possibility that videos like this can be created using AI â and that as such it can’t be considered truly confirmed until there’s an official reveal â the general consensus from Persona fans appears to be belief that the footage is legitimate, though there’s debate over whether it’s actual gameplay or an internal pitch video to get a remake greenlit. Neither Sega nor Atlus has confirmed that a remake of the original Persona is in development, but one of the series’ producers was recently speaking about the possibility of one . In August, Persona 4 Revival producer Kazuhisa Wada was asked by Gamer Braves whether fans would ever see Persona and Persona 2 remakes, or Atlusâs focus was shifting entirely to Persona 6 once Persona 4 Revival is released. âAt this point, I canât say for sure,â Wada replied. âBut personally, I think itâs something we should definitely do. I think we have to do it.â The first game in the series, Revelations: Persona, was released on the PS1 in 1996, and later ported to PSP in 2009 with an updated UI, increased battle speed, balancing adjustments and a new soundtrack. This was followed by Persona 2: Innocent Sin and Persona 2: Eternal Punishment, two separate games released on PS1 in 1999 and 2000 respectively. Both games were ported to PSP in 2011 and 2012 respectively. Since then, Persona, Persona 2: Innocent Sin and Persona 2: Eternal Punishment have generally lain dormant as Atlus continues to favour the more recent third, fourth and fifth entries in the series, which have received numerous remakes and spin-offs.

sources.text: From grappling mutants to cyborg tanks, discover which kaiju is right for you. With its giant-sized fanbase, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has plenty of players ready to get tooth, nail, and claw stuck into its PlayStation 5 release on November 3. Although it would be understandable that newcomers might feel a little intimidated choosing between 12 world crushing kaiju, each with their own stats, moveset, and special abilities. Never fear – we have the rundown on which colossus matches your playstyle to ensure you’re the true king of the monsters. Ideal for: Players who want to dive straight in. The face which sank a thousand ships. Godzilla is the iconic kaiju who all other kaiju want to be, beat, or be friends with. As the game’s default character, the giant lizard is balanced for newbies and veterans alike, with a high amount of starting health and decent all-round stats. Godzilla also possesses a tail useful enough for a mighty wake-up strike when he’s downed, and some fairly swift claws, so many of his melee combos are effective for beginners. But don’t rely too much on his high-energy pulse – while it’s formidable, the slow charge leaves him open to counters. Similarly, ranged attackers can take advantage of his relatively sluggish projectiles, so close that distance or you’ll be heading back to Monster Island with your giant tail between your legs. Ideal for: Players annoyed at their friend for picking Heisei Godzilla. In terms of film history, Godzilla 2000 is a more modern incarnation of the legendary lizard, reflecting a new era for the new millennium. Although he’s arguably a slightly more vulnerable version of his Heisei predecessor. As a result, while Godzilla 2000 is a bit faster than his kaiju shoto fighter twin, he’s not quite as strong. He’s still fairly well balanced and arguably easier to use than Heisei, so makes for a solid alternative. And his distinctive purple dorsal plates look pretty cool, too. Ideal for: Players who want to control the battlefield. There’s a reason why this fearsome three-headed beast is seen as Godzilla’s archnemesis. Giant wings, gravity beams, and a desire to annihilate humanity, the threat of King Ghidorah should never be taken lightly. Given his monstrous size it shouldn’t be a surprise that the ‘supreme ruler of the cosmos’ isn’t the fastest kaiju on the block, but he’s resilient and a perfect ‘zoning’ character, capable of keeping foes at a distance with a variety of projectiles. His flight is a little limited due to its energy drain, but it’s balanced by a lightning blast that has no charge while airborne. However, despite his colossal wings, Ghidorah’s lack of arms and stubby legs makes him a poor melee fighter. Ideal for: Players who think defense is the best offense. He might look a bit like Godzooky with more spikes, but mutant dinosaur Anguirus is one of Godzilla’s most loyal allies – even if his track record against other kaiju hasn’t been the best in the movies. The Monster Island citizen is fast and aggressive, but his low power and lack of long-range attacks means Anguirus is best utilized as a counter-attack specialist. His block might be on the slow side due to its turning animation, but it actually damages an attacking opponent due to Anguirus’ rear spines. With his high defense and solid grappling skills, this mutant shouldn’t be underestimated. Ideal for: Players who love to hit and run. Given its status as a guardian to the ancient underground civilisation of Seatopia, Megalon is more of an antagonist than an out-and-out villain in Godzilla lore. While not quite as domineering as its colossal rivals, the subterranean kaiju is still capable of putting a hurt on with its drill-like appendages. Megalon’s primary advantage is its tunnelling skill which not only allows it to avoid attacks, but also pop-up and grab opponents. Even though burrowing uses energy, it still makes Megalon a difficult fighter to pin down, especially when used in tandem with its myriad of electricity attacks. On the flip side, Megalon isn’t the most durable of beasts with below average defense. Stick and move, or die. Ideal for: Players wanting to attack with deadly speed. One of the most sadistic fighters to hail from M Space Hunter Nebula, cyborg kaiju Gigan is easily one of Godzilla’s more vicious adversaries. Despite being defeated multiple times, the hook-clawed Gigan just keeps coming back for more. Unsurprisingly, Gigan’s tenacious approach makes him perfect for aggressive rushdown tactics. He’s not only swift, but his teleportation ability gives him incredible range and evasion skills. And those hooks aren’t for decoration either, delivering damage-heavy edged strikes. His Laser Eye is a little unwieldy, and he’s vulnerable to energy attacks, but Gigan remains a versatile option for anyone wanting a decent melee and range mix-up. Giant wings, clawed hands, taloned feet… this mutant crustacean almost has it all. Which is to say, Destoroyah is one of the more powerful creatures in the game with brutal physical assaults and a wide variety of high-damage – and often unblockable – energy attacks that truly make him the perfect mid-range monster. But there’s a cost. Destoroyah’s best abilities are extremely power hungry, so without them he’s potentially ineffective given how painfully slow his movement is. Ideal for: Players wanting speed above all else. sources.title: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered Review
sources.text: The first time I ever saw Japan's most famous kaiju on the big screen was in Godzilla 2000: Millennium. Like any nine-year-old kid, I was obsessed with Big G. I read the Dark Horse comics, and I taped all the movies I could on TV. Things were different then; Godzilla was a big deal, but theatrical releases for Godzilla films were incredibly rare in the States If you saw those movies, it was on TV and they were dubbed or edited versions released under different titles like Godzilla: King of the Monsters or Godzilla vs. The Sea Monster. After Godzilla 2000 underperformed, it took another five years for the series to see a theatrical release in the U.S. – and into that void stomped 2002’s Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee. It was the perfect mix of subject matter (big monsters who were super into professional wrestling), genre (3D fighting game), and time period (licensed games were still, like… a thing). It was the kind of game that could dominate a pizza-filled sleepover weekend or become your personality for an entire summer. One friend’s parents bought it for them, and that copy became communal: a holy thing, carried from place to place. Maybe it’s fitting that it’s back now in the form of Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered, 24 years later. The world (and Godzilla) has changed a lot, but original developer Pipeworks is still at the helm. It somehow feels just as relevant now as it did then, just in different ways, and revisiting it was a joy even removed from the nostalgia. There is no one-to-one equivalent for what Destroy All Monsters Melee is, but the idea is pretty simple: you pick one of 12 monsters from Godzilla’s history (up through Godzilla 2000) – Godzilla, Gigan, Megalon, Ghidorah, etc. – then choose a real-world city or iconic Godzilla location to battle it out in. You’ll fight in classic rubber suit wrestling style while dodging environmental hazards, knocking down buildings, throwing rocks and skyscrapers at each other, and squashing the annoying military forces that really would prefer if you made a mess somewhere else. Last kaiju standing wins. Despite the name, this isn't a straight remaster. You're not just looking at uprezzed models. It looks fantastic while also maintaining the “these are guys in rubber suits drop-kicking each other” vibe that defines the films it’s based on. The audio pulls its weight, too – the soundtrack has the booming authority you'd expect from a Godzilla film, buildings crumble and collapse spectacularly, beam attacks sound powerful and painful, the radio calls from military forces in the area let you know where they’ll be focusing their fire, and the announcer is having a blast. And the monsters, of course, sound like themselves. And yeah, Godzilla makes The Noise, just like you remember, even if it’s your first time here. All of this is held together by a spit-and-duct-tape story that's just there to get you brawling: see, there's this alien race called the Vortaak. They're little green men with funky helmets, straight-from-the-‘50s fashion sense, flying saucers, and more than a little ego. They're here to take over the Earth, and what better way to do it than mind control the frankly absurd number of kaiju that are just hanging around, ready to smash a city at a moment's notice? Unfortunately for them, whichever Monster you pick breaks free of their mind control and decides the Earth is worth saving. Driving off the Vortaak means KOing the other monsters. All in a day's work, really. That's Adventure mode, which is one of several single-player options for you to rearrange cities in. You've also got Destruction for the score chasers, where you have to wreck a city in a time limit, a souped-up Adventure mode for monsters who are at a higher level and have better stats (which you gain from experience you earn as you play certain modes), and Survival, which is exactly what it sounds like. Listen, you can count the number of fighting games with good single-player modes on two hands (and several of those have the words “Soul Calibur” in their titles), but what's on offer here is solid if not spectacular. You only start with four monsters and a few stages unlocked, but Pipeworks has smartly reworked this remaster so you can unlock the rest in pretty much whatever order you like. You just have to meet the requirements, which you do by playing, following rumors, and unlocking research, and you can swap what you're focusing on whenever you like. On the one hand, yeah, it's super satisfying to unlock Ghidorah because it's Ghidorah – as soon as he stops being a silhouette I can't select and starts being a gloriously golden three-headed dragon I can take into battle, some lizard part of my brain gets very happy because I can't wait to fly around and shoot lightning with that sumbitch. On the other hand, it's mad annoying to see Rodan or Ghidorah or Mecha Godzilla in Adventure mode and have the 12-year-old who lives in my head put down his slice of pizza long enough to be like “hell yeah, I wanna play that one” and then realize I can't, especially in multiplayer. Does it give you more reasons to keep playing? Absolutely, and this stuff was part and parcel of the original experience. But man, sometimes you just wanna throw down with your friends without worrying about unlocks, you know? Multiplayer, of course, is really what Destroy All Monsters Melee is designed for, and I'm so happy that Pipeworks has added online play in addition to the returning local options. It even works really well! Most of the matches I played pre-release were smooth, though I did suffer a few disconnects. (Almost all of which happened when I was winning or doing well – I'm not saying my boy Lucas is a fraud or anything, but…) It's here, in the multiplayer, that Destroy All Monsters Melee really shines. People will tell you, naively, that this is a button masher with no depth. These people are foolish and wrong, and if this were a Godzilla movie, they'd got a drama

sources.title: Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered decepciona na acessibilidade, apesar da diversão
sources.text: Lançamentos de games em NOVEMBRO de 2026 - Calendário VOXL Além do aguardado GTA 6, novembro traz remake de Ocarina of Time e mais de 30 jogos. Confira as estreias do mês. Crédito: Voxl Sempre fui um grande fã de kaijus e de toda essa cultura de criaturas e robôs gigantes. Por isso, quando soube que Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee receberia uma versão remasterizada, fiquei bastante empolgado. Sempre tive vontade de jogar esse clássico, lançado originalmente em 2002 para Nintendo GameCube e Xbox, mas nunca tive acesso às plataformas necessárias na época. Agora, mais de duas décadas depois, finalmente tenho a oportunidade de conhecer esse jogo em uma versão voltada para os consoles e computadores atuais. Com a chegada de Godzilla Minus Zero , sequência de Godzilla Minus One prevista para novembro de 2026, o momento também parece propício para resgatar um clássico da porradaria entre monstros gigantes. Afinal, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee tem aquela energia dos jogos que você reúne os primos para jogar, sem compromisso com o realismo ou com uma narrativa complexa, apenas para trocar golpes, destruir cenários e dar boas risadas. É um tipo de diversão descompromissada que não se leva tão a sério — e isso faz parte do seu charme. Desenvolvido originalmente pela Pipeworks Studios, o jogo coloca kaijus conhecidos da franquia em confrontos nos quais prédios e outros elementos do cenário também fazem parte da pancadaria. A versão remasterizada busca preservar essa experiência, atualizando a apresentação visual e levando o combate para plataformas modernas, além de incluir recursos como partidas online. Mas, quando um jogo clássico retorna depois de tantos anos, surge uma questão importante: por que modernizar apenas os gráficos e os recursos técnicos? Relançamentos também são oportunidades para rever aspectos da experiência que vão além da resolução das imagens ou do desempenho. Controles mais flexíveis, opções gráficas ajustáveis e recursos de acessibilidade podem fazer a diferença para que mais pessoas consigam aproveitar um jogo. Isso é especialmente relevante em títulos de ação, nos quais acompanhar vários personagens na tela, identificar ataques em meio a explosões, interpretar informações da interface e executar comandos no momento certo pode representar uma barreira para jogadores com deficiência. É com essa perspectiva que analiso Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered . Além de revisitar um clássico que sempre tive vontade de experimentar, quero entender quais recursos de acessibilidade estão disponíveis nessa nova versão, quais barreiras permanecem e até que ponto o relançamento aproveita a oportunidade de adaptar essa experiência às necessidades de jogadores com deficiência. Afinal, destruir cidades com monstros gigantes pode ser uma diversão para muita gente, mas essa diversão só será realmente acessível quando mais jogadores puderem participar dela. Vale ressaltar que a acessibilidade é uma experiência individual e se aplica de maneira diferente a cada pessoa, de acordo com suas necessidades e características. Portanto, as impressões apresentadas nesta análise partem da minha experiência pessoal como pessoa com baixa visão. Meu objetivo é destacar os recursos de acessibilidade presentes no jogo, explicar como eles podem contribuir para uma experiência mais inclusiva e apontar as barreiras que encontrei durante os testes. Essas observações não pretendem representar a experiência de todas as pessoas com deficiência, mas contribuir para que mais jogadores conheçam as possibilidades e limitações oferecidas pelo título. Aviso de transparência: Esta análise foi realizada com uma chave de acesso antecipado disponibilizada pela equipe de Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered para PS5, antes do lançamento oficial do jogo. O título é desenvolvido pela Pipeworks Studios e publicado pela Atari. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered oferece legendas, mas não permite alterar o tamanho ou personalizar sua apresentação. Também não há opções de legendas ocultas ( closed captions ) que identifiquem sons importantes do ambiente e dos combates, o que pode dificultar o acompanhamento das partidas por jogadores surdos ou com deficiência auditiva. Um dos pontos mais decepcionantes é a falta de opções para personalizar os controles. Mesmo sendo um relançamento para plataformas modernas, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered não oferece remapeamento de comandos nem ajustes mais detalhados para adaptar a jogabilidade às necessidades de cada pessoa. Essa limitação pesa especialmente em um jogo de luta e ação no qual é necessário executar diferentes comandos durante confrontos movimentados. Sem a possibilidade de reorganizar os botões, jogadores com deficiência motora podem encontrar dificuldades para realizar determinadas ações ou simplesmente não conseguir configurar os comandos de uma maneira confortável. A ausência de alternativas também reduz a flexibilidade para quem precisa de uma configuração específica por questões de mobilidade ou coordenação. É frustrante que uma versão remasterizada não aproveite a oportunidade para incluir recursos tão importantes. Atualizar os gráficos e levar o jogo a plataformas atuais não é suficiente para modernizar a experiência quando os controles continuam sem opções básicas de personalização. A vibração do controle pode ser ativada ou desativada, mas esse ajuste pontual está longe de compensar a falta de remapeamento. Nas configurações de áudio, o jogo permite ajustar separadamente o volume da música, dos efeitos sonoros e das vozes dos personagens. Essa divisão oferece algum controle sobre a mixagem, mas não é acompanhada de recursos específicos que ajudem jogadores com deficiência auditiva a identificar os acontecimentos durante as partidas. O título não apresenta indicadores visuais para sons relevantes, que poderiam ajudar a sinalizar ataques e outros eventos importantes. Em meio à destruição dos cenários e à movimenta

sources.title: Valve’s Cancelled Portal Prequel F-Stop Has Leaked
sources.text: F-Stop , Valveâs cancelled 2007 Portal prequel, has leaked onlineâand yes, itâs fully playable. If youâve heard of F-Stop , you donât need me to tell you why this is a huge deal. But if you havenât, then youâre in for quite the history lesson. In 2007, Valve spent three months on a project that Gabe Newell would later dub the Directed Design Experiments. Now, Iâm not going to attempt to tell the story better than the folks at the Half-Life wiki have before, so hereâs the short version: during these three months, Valve broke off into five teams. Each team designed and partially created a video game âexperiment,â and the fifth was dubbed â F-Stop .â F-Stop was conceptualised as a prequel to Portal , and the gameplay revolved around using an experimental Aperture Science camera to mess with perspectives and solve puzzles. Gabe Newell himself was very taken with the project, but playtesters were less thrilled. Ultimately, F-Stop was scrapped, and some of its dialogue, characters, and mechanics were reworked into Portal 2 . Well, consider it scrapped no longer, as thanks to the efforts of several leakers and the Valve Cut Content team , F-Stop is now playable in (almost) its entirety. If youâre curious as to how this leaked, the long answer is that itâs actually a combination of three separate leaks. Some of you might remember that in late August, roughly 13 terabytes of Steam depot data leaked online . The leak, dubbed Steam2, seemingly contained almost every Steam depot from 2003 to 2013 and, most surprisingly, assets for F-Stop . However, while the Steam2 leak included the majority of F-Stopâs assets, it did not include F-Stopâs source code or its mapsrc data (Valveâs folder name for its map source code data). It appears both of these final pieces of the F-Stop puzzle were leaked via the Valve Cut Content projectâs Discord server over the past 48 hours. According to the mods in the server, the person who leaked the F-Stop mapsrc initially asked for $1,000, but, for whatever reason, just ended up giving them away for free anyway. The Valve Cut Content team has verified the map files’ authenticity, and the community has combined all three of the puzzle pieces into the end result: a fully playable version of F-Stop . Those who have played it are reporting that while there appear to be a few missing assets and dialogue lines here and there, itâs essentially 99 percent complete. Unsurprising, as I’m sure Valve would have added a little more polish if they ever planned to release this officially, but hey, letâs be realââ99 percent completeâ is a hell of a lot more than the 0 percent complete we had this time last week. sources.text: Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media. Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media. Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop . Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together, according to Kotaku . Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2 . But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way. The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “ Directed Design Experiments ,” which, according to The Half-Life & Portal Encyclopedia, was a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments. sources.title: Valve's canceled Portal follow-up F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to that 12TB Steam leak and some dedicated fans
sources.text: The prequel was canceled because playtesters were confused about why it didn't have the Portal gun F-Stop – the canceled Valve project that was the original Portal follow-up – has leaked online and is fully playable after being found in the massive Steam leak earlier this year. Back in August 12TB of Steam data from 2003 and 2013 dropped online which featured a ton of builds of Valve titles like Portal 2, Left 4 Dead, and Counter Strike: Global Offensive. This data was apparently "hidden in plain sight, but with no protection whatsoever," and was easily accessible without hacking the whole time, proving to be a treasure trove for Valve fanatics, with early Portal 2 builds featuring bullet time being uncovered. And unless Half Life 2: Episode 3 is found anytime soon, the true holy grail of this leak may have been found. As reported by Kotaku , users in the Valve Cut Content project’s Discord have managed to find the game's source code and map data, meaning that F-Stop is fully playable. YouTube user ToothpasteVixen uploaded the intro to the game – featuring earlier narration from a JK Simmons-less Cave Johnson – which will give you a good idea of the concept for those unaware, but to put it simply, it almost feels like an earlier take on the 2019 puzzle game Superliminal where taking photos allows you to manipulate the environment. F-Stop was one of five projects coming from what Gabe Newell described as "Directed Design Experiments," where Valve's production was shut down for a few months which would have the company's teams participate in what is effectively a massive game jam. F-Stop was one of the standout projects from it, with Newell asking the team behind it to develop it into a prequel to Portal. Ultimately, as per Portal 2 - the Final Hours, the project was canceled after playtesters didn't react entirely positively – namely, questioning why a Portal follow-up did not include the Portal Gun – but now, 15 years after the actual Portal 2 was released and with no sequel in sight, you can play a sort of new Portal experience. sources.title: Xbox Game Pass: por que o sucesso das assinaturas preocupa os estúdios?
sources.text: O Xbox Game Pass mudou a maneira como muitos jogadores consomem videogames. Em vez de comprar cada título individualmente, os assinantes têm acesso a um catálogo que reúne produções independentes e grandes lançamentos. Para o consumidor, a proposta é atraente. Mas, para quem desenvolve e publica jogos, a situação é mais complexa. Afinal, disponibilizar um título em um serviço de assinatura ajuda a conquistar público ou prejudica suas vendas? Essa discussão ganhou força em 2023, quando documentos apresentados pela Microsoft à autoridade britânica de concorrência (CMA), durante a análise da aquisição da Activision Blizzard , revelaram que a empresa identificou uma redução nas vendas de jogos após sua entrada no Game Pass. Segundo os documentos apresentados à CMA, análises internas da Microsoft apontaram uma queda nas vendas de determinados jogos nos 12 meses seguintes à inclusão no serviço. O percentual exato não foi divulgado publicamente. A informação contrasta com declarações anteriores de Phil Spencer, chefe da divisão Xbox , que havia defendido que a presença de jogos no catálogo poderia aumentar sua popularidade e impulsionar as vendas. Entretanto, os dois cenários não são necessariamente incompatíveis. Um jogo pode conquistar novos jogadores e ganhar visibilidade inicialmente, mas registrar menos compras individuais ao longo do tempo. O impacto também depende do tamanho do estúdio, do contrato negociado e do comportamento do público. Para desenvolvedoras independentes, serviços como o Game Pass podem funcionar como uma vitrine. Estar disponível em um catálogo de assinatura permite alcançar jogadores que talvez não comprassem o título separadamente. Por outro lado, existe o risco de parte desse público deixar de adquirir o jogo, especialmente quando ele chega ao serviço no lançamento. O modelo também envolve questões financeiras. Dependendo do acordo, a receita obtida pela desenvolvedora pode compensar a redução nas vendas tradicionais. Em outros casos, a participação pode ser menos vantajosa. Por isso, não existe uma resposta única sobre os benefícios das assinaturas para a indústria. Apesar das discussões, o Game Pass não eliminou a compra tradicional de videogames. Os dois modelos continuam coexistindo, oferecendo diferentes maneiras de acessar os mesmos produtos. Para os jogadores, as assinaturas podem representar economia e a oportunidade de experimentar títulos desconhecidos. Para os estúdios, a decisão exige avaliar alcance, receita e possíveis impactos nas vendas. O debate, portanto, não é simplesmente sobre o Game Pass ser bom ou ruim. A questão é entender se um modelo vantajoso para o consumidor também consegue ser sustentável para quem produz os jogos . E essa resposta pode variar bastante de um lançamento para outro. sources.title: Anthropic Blocks AI Game Clones in Claude Opus Update
sources.text: Anthropic has issued an update for Claude that puts a stop to the AI-generated game clones that have filled platforms like Steam. The term 'AI slop' is something we've heard a lot in the past few years, but it became especially prevalent in the gaming community after Valve launched Steam Next Fest earlier this month. PC users quickly launched complaints that their feeds had been filled with low-effort clones not only of pre-existing games but even some titles that had only just released their own demos. As players trudged through the slop, developers faced a reality that threw months or even years of hard work into jeopardy. Some, including Drunken Goddess Reflux developer Alliance Arts and Who You , even took action by canceling their Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. It's a situation that rapidly spun out of control, prompting a response from Valve itself as it said it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem." ANTHROPIC IS CRACKING DOWN ON VIDEO GAME REWRITES 🚨 Claude Code picked up a new rule around Oct 27, sent from Anthropic’s servers under a flag called "tengu_heron_brook". There’s no setting to turn it off. The full rule: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.” Is this the end of game rewrites, modding and everything in between? As reported by Game Developer , X/Twitter user Chasm was one of the first to share evidence of tech company Anthropic taking action against video game copycats. Based on their findings, Claude, the company's AI assistant, recently received an update featuring a new rule. The full rule can be read below: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." When reached for comment by Game Developer, Anthropic pointed to a post shared by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff. Osmani's explanation can be read below: "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Whether there was a specific event or reason that prompted Anthropic to make these changes is unclear. Game developers and game enjoyers will no doubt find comfort in Anthropic's changes, though it's worth noting that how impactful any of this will be remains to be seen. At the very least, those who use Claude to rip ideas directly from those who used their minds and time to bring them to life should have a tougher time trying to profit off of the work of others. The industry is struggling to come to grips with artificial intelligence. Some, such as Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, have insisted that Valve should stray from asking developers to disclose games utilizing generative AI materials . Others, including Super Smash Bros. mastermind Masahiro Sakurai, have compared AI-generated games to "low-quality goods." The developers behind VRChat, meanwhile, recently came under fire for how they are handling AI content . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games , and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use . Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies. The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen . AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser . However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo. Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

sources.text: Lançamentos de games em NOVEMBRO de 2026 - Calendário VOXL Além do aguardado GTA 6, novembro traz remake de Ocarina of Time e mais de 30 jogos. Confira as estreias do mês. Crédito: Voxl O ano de 2026 está bastante movimentado no mercado de games, mas novembro promete ser um dos meses mais marcantes da história recente dos videogames. De um lado, temos Grand Theft Auto 6, um dos lançamentos mais aguardados de todos os tempos e que chega após anos de expectativa e adiamentos. Do outro, a Nintendo prepara o retorno de um dos maiores clássicos da indústria: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, em um remake que promete dividir os holofotes com a aventura da Rockstar. A proximidade entre os dois lançamentos já rendeu comparações com o fenômeno “Barbenheimer”, nome dado ao encontro inesperado entre Barbie e Oppenheimer nos cinemas, em julho de 2023. Na época, os filmes de propostas completamente diferentes transformaram a disputa nas bilheterias em um evento cultural, com espectadores abraçando a ideia de assistir às duas produções. Agora, a indústria dos games tem sua própria versão dessa disputa. Enquanto GTA 6 chega em 19 de novembro, o remake de Ocarina of Time está previsto para 5 de novembro, no começo do mês, colocando duas das franquias mais importantes dos videogames em rota de colisão. No entanto, essa “disputa” pode acabar sendo mais amigável do que o esperado por um motivo importante: o mercado é gigante e os títulos estreiam em plataformas bem diferentes. A comparação com o fenômeno Barbenheimer ganhou ainda mais força depois que o programa Saturday Night Live apresentou uma esquete sobre o confronto durante o quadro Weekend Update. Na brincadeira, os protagonistas dos dois jogos, Jason e Link, aparecem conversando com o apresentador Colin Jost sobre a expectativa em torno dos lançamentos de novembro. Interpretado por Marcello Hernández, Jason representa o lado caótico de GTA 6, descrevendo um dia que envolve fuga da prisão, assalto a banco, roubo de carros e até o sequestro de um Boeing Dreamliner. Já Link, interpretado por Mikey Day, apresenta uma rotina consideravelmente mais tranquila em Hyrule, envolvendo a compra de feijões mágicos e uma música tocada na ocarina. A diferença entre os personagens resume bem a proposta da comparação. Enquanto Jason encerra sua participação prometendo “destruição, caos e sexo”, Link oferece “quebra-cabeças e combate leve” como alternativa para os jogadores. A chegada de GTA 6 tem sido um dos principais fatores de influência no calendário de lançamentos de 2026. Diversas desenvolvedoras e distribuidoras evitaram colocar seus grandes jogos na mesma janela do título da Rockstar, temendo perder espaço e atenção do público para um lançamento que deve movimentar toda a indústria. O impacto já aparece no planejamento de outras empresas. Alguns jogos tiveram suas datas alteradas para fugir da concorrência, enquanto outros projetos foram empurrados para 2027. Afinal, GTA 6 não disputa apenas vendas: o jogo também deve dominar as conversas nas redes sociais, transmissões ao vivo, vídeos e a cobertura especializada durante semanas. Confira 26 minutos de gameplay de GTA 6, que chega em 19 de novembro no PS5 e Xbox Series S/X Olhar Estendido divulgado pela Rockstar Games apresenta detalhes da jogabilidade do aguardado Grand Theft Auto VI. A Nintendo, por outro lado, parece disposta a aproveitar a proximidade com uma estratégia diferente. Em vez de tentar competir diretamente com a Rockstar no mesmo dia, a empresa posicionou Ocarina of Time duas semanas antes do lançamento de GTA 6, apostando na força de uma franquia que atravessa gerações. Com isso, a empresa pode ganhar as atenções dos seus fãs e usuários fieis antes da estreia do aguardado game da Rockstar Games. Afinal, o Switch 2 já possui mais de 23 milhões de unidades vendidas e não receberá GTA 6, abrindo caminho para o sucesso de Zelda na plataforma. O peso de GTA 6 no mercado é difícil de ignorar. O novo capítulo da franquia é apontado por relatos da indústria como o videogame mais caro já produzido e promete levar os jogadores de volta a Vice City, agora integrada ao estado fictício de Leonida. A Rockstar também confirmou que o mapa será aproximadamente duas vezes maior que o de GTA 5, com um nível maior de detalhes. O lançamento também deve ser um acontecimento comercial fora do padrão. Executivos da indústria já projetam que parte dos jogadores poderá até tirar folga do trabalho para aproveitar a estreia, algo que ajuda a dimensionar a expectativa em torno do projeto. O jogo aposta na nostalgia e na força de um dos jogos mais importantes da história da Nintendo para ganhar a atenção do público. Lançado originalmente em 1998, o título marcou época ao estabelecer referências para aventuras em três dimensões e permanece entre as experiências mais celebradas da franquia The Legend of Zelda. sources.title: Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3: clássico da franquia completa 25 anos
sources.text: O jogo marcou um ponto de virada no que foi a primeira transição de plataforma da série. O retorno da trupe de skatistas contava com 13 profissionais, mas, infelizmente para nós brasileiros, Bob Burnquist ficou de fora pela primeira e única vez até Proving Ground. Isso aconteceu porque Bob havia fechado um contrato para aparecer em outro jogo, o ESPN X Games Skateboarding. A ausência do único latino abriu espaço para um dos nomes mais conhecidos dos anos 2000: Bam Margera. Publicado pela Activision (sob o selo Activision O2), o título chegou ao PlayStation, Nintendo 64, PC, Mac, Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, PlayStation 2, Xbox e GameCube. Boa parte desses lançamentos aconteceu ainda em 2001, mas algumas plataformas receberam o jogo apenas no ano seguinte. A desenvolvedora original, Neversoft, ficou responsável justamente pelas versões dos consoles mais modernas, deixando outras empresas como Shaba Games, Vicarious Visions e HotGen incumbidas das versões para PSX, GBA e GBC respectivamente. A versão do primeiro console da Sony foi portada pela Edge of Reality para o N64, já os ports feitos para PC e Mac (que foram baseados no game para PS2, Xbox e GC) foram de incumbência da Gearbox Software e da Beenox respectivamente. Outra curiosidade é que THPS3 foi oficialmente o último jogo lançado para o console de 64 bits da Nintendo (agosto de 2002), que havia sido descontinuado quatro meses antes. O game foi desenvolvido no motor gráfico RenderWare, criado em 1993 pela Criterion Games. No entanto, as versões do PlayStation e do Nintendo 64 rodavam na mesma engine de Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2, a Apocalypse. Para se ter uma idéia, a RenderWare foi utilizada até a geração do PlayStation 4, e foi usada em clássicos como a trilogia 3D do GTA (III, Vice City e San Andreas). A Neversoft começou o terceiro milênio com os dois pés na porta ao tratar do novo Tony Hawk. Aproveitando as possibilidades das plataformas mais modernas, a empresa dedicou-se a criar muitas coisas novas para a franquia. A primeira delas, que mais marcou, foi o revert. A manobra permitia que os combos continuassem quando o skatista entrava em um quarter pipe (as manobras aéreas), apertando o botão quando encostasse na rampa ao cair e então emendar em um manual. Essa novidade foi tão importante que em jogos posteriores, como Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater HD, a DLC com mapas do terceiro jogo chamava-se Revert Pack. Até mesmo o primeiro remake recente, Tony Hawk’s 1+2, continha a manobra disponível, apesar de ela ainda não existir nos originais. Outra novidade que virou um marco da série foram os Hidden Combos. Basicamente eram variações de manobras feitas durante um manual, um flip ou um grind. Essas manobras foram inspiradas especialmente nas competições de freestyle, em que Rodney Mullen dava show no final da década de 1970 e nos anos 1980. Nessas competições, Mullen usava diversas variações do manual, indo para manobras como casper, anti-casper, handstand, entre outros; tudo isso sem perder o equilíbrio e sem “resetar” a sequência. No jogo, cada variação aumenta o multiplicador de pontos do combo nos casos de manual e grind. O flip trick apenas permitia uma nova manobra (como double kickflip) que valia mais pontos e gastava um tempo maior para ser realizada. Por falar nas manobras nos corrimãos, o balanço para grind e lip tricks foi adicionado ao game. Similar ao de manual, permitia um controle melhor e mais preciso para estender combos ao conseguir equilibrar o skatista. Essa foi outra ideia que permeou para sempre os jogos da franquia, uma vez que era mais complicado de manter o equilíbrio nos jogos anteriores (o personagem ia pendendo pra um lado somente, sem mais indícios). Algumas das ideias menores implementadas foram a inserção de pedestres e NPCs nos mapas, a possibilidade de criar uma skatista feminina (em THPS 2 só era possível criar atletas masculinos) e a remoção do Big Drop, permitindo quedas de alturas imensas sem perder o combo. Por fim, a principal novidade explorada pelo marketing do jogo foi o modo online. O que hoje é comum e avaliado como básico para qualquer título, naquela época a história era outra. Afinal, o PlayStation 2 não possuía modem embutido, o que já criava uma barreira. Além disso, era a época da conexão discada, a banda larga apenas começava a dar os primeiros passos no comércio para clientes finais nos grandes mercados. Antes do lançamento do adaptador de rede do console, era possível jogar online com adaptadores ethernet USB. A versão do Xbox, ironicamente, não possuía uma forma de jogar pela internet, apesar de o console contar com modem embutido. Apesar de ter contado com várias inovações, o núcleo principal do jogo permanecia o mesmo. Afinal, time que está ganhando não se mexe, e os jogos da série até então foram muito elogiados por todos. A gameplay básica permanecia a mesma para movimentação, para a execução das manobras, o funcionamento de gaps, enfim, esses aspectos foram apenas aprimorados. A proposta do game era a mesma: fases com dois minutos para realizar dez objetivos, que podiam ser feitos em várias tentativas, e outros níveis com o campeonato valendo a medalha de ouro, que consistia em três chances de um minuto cada para obter a maior nota. As fases eram liberadas conforme objetivos iam sendo realizados, ou conquistar uma medalha de bronze ao menos. Começava com Foundry, Canada, Rio de Janeiro (torneio), Suburbia, Airport, Skater Island (torneio), Los Angeles e Tokyo (torneio). As versões da sexta geração contavam ainda com Cruise Ship (também com dez objetivos) e mais versões remasterizadas da Warehouse, Burnside e Roswell. Os skatistas são basicamente os mesmos de THPS 2, exceto pela mudança mencionada anteriormente. A versão japonesa ainda recebeu quatro novos profissionais do país. sources.title: Tony Hawk Kicked Out Of Park While Trying To Recreate Pro Skater 3
sources.text: PlayStation 2 skateboarding Tony Hawk's Pro Skater Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4 Tony Hawk, skateboard legend, video game superstar and the last one to die in the great uprising , has inspired the culture for generations. Since Neversoft put him on the PlayStation in 1999, Hawk has been a household name, the video game series inspiring boarders on the couch and halfpipe alike. Looking to celebrate the 25th anniversary of Tony Hawkâs Pro Skater 3 , he traveled to the real world Los Angeles park recreated within the game. Only to be escorted out by security. “Happy 25th THPS3!” Posted the Birdman himself . “We got kicked out of Pershing Square while shooting this today.” Though unnamed in the game, the Los Angeles stage of Tony Hawkâs Pro Skater 3 is clearly inspired by Pershing Square, a business park in the cityâs financial district. With its distinctive modernist features from architect Ricardo Legorreta, the stone crescent benches and large red orbs made for a slick backdrop in the 2001 extreme sports game. It still remains in the city today, largely unchanged, as well as the nearby car wash with a big blue obelisk. As such, recreating the beloved video game should have made for easy content. To the Ramones’ Blitzkrieg Bop , Hawk rolls through Pershing Square, revisiting the sights, recreating the worbling idle stance of his virtual avatar. Leaving most of the tricks to his PlayStation self, Hawk and his team could only film so much before being ejected from the site by security. “She [security] just shooâd us away,” posted Hawk. “It was very anticlimactic.” The third entry in the series was the first to hit the PlayStation 2. To this day itâs considered not just one of the best in the series, but is tied with Grand Theft Auto 3 as Metacritic’s best on the console . The game was remade in 2025, part of Iron Galaxyâs Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3 + 4 bundle. While the first set was met with a ticker-tape parade, the secondâs reception was a touch milder . Fans young and old continue to be frustrated as getting new, no nonsense entries in any legacy skateboard series feels like pulling teeth, when they could be losing them off a botched rail grind instead. sources.title: Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online
sources.text: Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online. The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit . It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake". Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload . There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style. Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment . Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats. How do you solve a problem like Persona 4 ? At Gamescom, we sat down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about the Persona 4 Remake , and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake.

sources.title: There’s Footage Running Around That Might Be A First Look At A Persona 1 Remake
sources.text: We now have an idea of what a Revelations: Persona remake could look like. There’s a video being passed around on the gaming leaks and rumors subreddit that purportedly contains footage of the first Persona game after it’s been hit with the Atlus remake-ification beam. It’s a short video, entirely in Japanese, that seems to depict a gaggle of teenagers trying to escape what looks like a haunted hospital. As the main character (referred to as “boy with earring”) turns a corner, he’s attacked by a monster and the video cuts to a battle sequence. Surprisingly, it looks like the protagonist from Persona 2 , Tatsuya Suou, makes an appearance in the battle, which also features a character who looks like Eriko Kirishima. Combat itself includes a highly stylized UI centered on the attacking character with options that include “persona,” “gun,” “sword,” “item,” and “defend,” as well as a turn order list and other info. There’s no confirmation that this is real footage from a P1 remake and as of publication time, the Reddit thread and the page where the video link is hosted have not yet been subject to any takedown notices. There’s speculation this video could be a mod or a project that was vibe-coded with AI, but comments throughout the Reddit thread say that if it is fake, it’s incredibly well-done. Some commenters, however, are too busy arguingÂ about whether or not it’s a good thing this “remake” looks reminiscent of Persona 5 and the remakes of Persona 3-4 , and not more like the original Persona game its supposedly based on. Earlier this year, Persona producer Wada Kazuhisa said in an interview that remaking the first entries in the series was something Atlus “ should definitely do .” He noted that game development technology has advanced to the point where “we can now create new cutscenes that are more immersive and realistic than before,” which is certainly evident in…well, whatever that is. stories.title: Hoyoverse’s Cozy Sim Petit Planet Coming to Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Hoyoverse’s Cozy Sim Petit Planet Coming to Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027
sources.text: Rejoice, Nintendo Switch 2 owners with a taste for the cozy, because Hoyoverse, the studio behind Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail, is bringing its new intergalactic life sim Petit Planet to Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027. The free-to-play game is already releasing on PC, iOS, and Android on December 4, 2026, but it never hurts to have more cute and cozy content on your Switch. The news came as part of a special update on the game from Hoyoverse, which also gave us a deep dive into some of the Petit Planet neighbors you can encounter, the home decor features, and some of the mini-games available as you live your life in Starsea. You start out taking care of your own planet, but can then explore the little islands in the skies around Starsea or visit the hub-style Galactic Bazaar for things like in-game auctions and community features. Petit Planet was announced back in September 2025, and IGN got to play it a few months later , with our writer describing it as Animal Crossing meets The Little Prince. "In my short time of about five hours with a preview of the closed beta, Petit Planet offered a charming, The Little Prince-themed take on Animal Crossing: New Horizons with an emphasis on clear progression and multiplayer. While these are two things some seemed to crave and were left empty in ACNH, the Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail studio may offer an answer – with potential caveats." The special update also revealed a bunch of chances for players to score pre-registration prizes as well as a "Launch a Planet" event on the game's official website that starts today. Rachel Weber is the Head of Editorial Development at IGN and an elder millennial. She's been a professional nerd since 2006 when she got her start on Official PlayStation Magazine in the UK, and has since worked for GamesIndustry.Biz, Rolling Stone and GamesRadar. She loves horror, horror movies, horror games, Red Dead Redemption 2, and her Love and Deepspace boyfriends.

sources.title: Petit Planet coming to Switch 2 in 2027
sources.text: miHoYo will release a Switch 2 version of free-to-play cosmic life simulation game Petit Planet in 2027, the developer announced. It will launch first for PC via Epic Games Store and client download, iOS via App Store , and Android via Google Play on December 4, as previously announced . In Petit Planet , players take on the role of Planet Tenders, journeying to the Starsea on the back of Oumuamua, a Starsea Spirit said to listen to the wishes in people’s hearts. On their very own planet, they plant a Luca Seed that gradually grows into a Luca Arbor, shaping the planet’s landscape, seasons, and ecosystem over time. Life on the planet is never lonely. Planet Coordinator Mobai and Starsea Racer Elsasani are the first to welcome each Planet Tender to their new home, with more Neighbors arriving over time, each with their own stories to tell. As players get to know their Neighbors, chance encounters can blossom into lasting friendships. Beyond life on their home planet, players can set sail across the Starsea to explore its scattered Islets , or head to the Galactic Bazaar to enjoy games, take part in auctions, and share their creations. To celebrate the upcoming launch, HoYoverse has prepared a series of events and rewards for Planet Tenders. A pre-registration lucky draw on the official website offers exciting prizes, while over 1,000 clothing and furniture items can be earned for free through regular gameplay. In the “Besties, Made to Match!” event, players who team up with two friends to pre-register will each receive an exclusive clothing item. Starting November 1, the special “Launch a Planet” event invites players to design their own planets on the official event website, with a chance to win surprise grand prizes. The first Petit Planet Seasonal Creation Event will kick off alongside the game’s launch, offering cash prizes, in-game rewards, and official merchandise for selected fan creations. After the special program, players can also visit Petit Planet ‘s official X account to receive a “Moving Guide” and enter for a chance to win a suitcase, gift cards, and an exclusive luggage tag.
